ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Abrupt regular tachycardia in infancy

A 3-month-old abruptly becomes irritable and feeds poorly. The monitor shows a fixed rate of 250/min with narrow QRS complexes and no clearly visible P waves. The rate does not vary with sleep or crying. Which rhythm best explains these findings?

  1. Sinus tachycardia
  2. Atrial fibrillation
  3. Complete atrioventricular block
  4. Ventricular fibrillation
  5. Supraventricular tachycardia
Answer and explanation

Supraventricular tachycardia

Abrupt onset, very regular rapid rhythm and absent discernible sinus P waves favor SVT.

Option explanations

Supraventricular tachycardia: Abrupt onset, very regular rapid rhythm and absent discernible sinus P waves favor SVT.

Sinus tachycardia: Sinus tachycardia generally varies and has identifiable sinus P waves.

Atrial fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation usually produces an irregular ventricular response.

Complete atrioventricular block: Complete block commonly produces a slow escape rhythm and atrioventricular dissociation.

Ventricular fibrillation: Ventricular fibrillation has chaotic activity without organized QRS complexes.
